title: Chemistry 11 — Chapter 8: The Dilution Series
description: A batch of stock solution needs to become a full dilution series before Friday — but first, the crystallized leftovers from last week need explaining.

mika.name: Ms. Mika Tan
mika.description: Has seen every solubility and dilution mistake a student can make, twice.

priya.name: Priya
priya.description: Mixed last week's batch and wants to know what went wrong.

solubility_chart.name: Solubility Curve Chart
solubility_chart.description: Grams of solute per 100 g water, plotted against temperature.

dilution_formula.name: Dilution Formula Card
dilution_formula.description: C1V1 = C2V2, for making a weaker solution from a stronger stock.

elements.text: I dissolved this fine when it was warm, and now there are crystals sitting at the bottom. Did I mess up the recipe?
Probably not the recipe — probably the dissolving process itself, and what happens to it as it cools.

elements.prompt: Mika hands you the solubility curve chart.

options.text: "Let's start with how dissolving actually works, then check the curve."
"The recipe's probably just wrong, let's remix it."

elements.text: Water is polar, and it dissolves other polar or ionic substances by surrounding each particle — for an ionic compound like this one, water's partially negative oxygen end pulls toward the cations and its partially positive hydrogen ends pull toward the anions, pulling the whole lattice apart. That's why 'like dissolves like.'

config.question: Which best explains why water dissolves an ionic compound like NaCl?

options.text: Water's polar molecules surround and stabilize the separated ions
Water is a nonpolar solvent, matching NaCl's nonpolar bonds
Ionic bonds are too weak to exist once formed
NaCl doesn't actually dissolve, it just floats apart

config.explanation: Water's polar molecules orient around each ion, stabilizing it in solution and pulling the ionic lattice apart.

config.prompt: Sort each pairing by whether it dissolves well, based on 'like dissolves like.'

elements.text: This compound's solubility curve shows it dissolves more at higher temperatures. Dissolve it hot, near the curve's limit, and cooling drops the solution below that limit — the solvent can't hold as much anymore, so the excess crystallizes back out. That's exactly what happened to your batch.

config.question: A solution is prepared hot, right at its saturation point on the solubility curve. What happens as it cools?

options.text: It becomes supersaturated for its new temperature, and excess solute crystallizes out
Nothing — solubility doesn't depend on temperature
The solute becomes more soluble as it cools
The solvent itself evaporates, concentrating the solution

config.explanation: Since less solute can stay dissolved at the lower temperature, the amount above the new saturation limit crystallizes out.

config.prompt: Order these solution states from least to most solute dissolved, relative to the saturation point.

items.text: Unsaturated — can still dissolve more solute
Supersaturated — holding more than the equilibrium maximum

elements.text: Molarity is the standard concentration unit here — moles of solute per liter of solution, mol/L.

config.prompt: Priya dissolves 2.0 mol of solute into 4.0 L of solution. What's the molarity, in mol/L? Just the number.

config.question: Molarity is expressed in which unit?

options.text: mol/L
g/mol
mol/kg
g/L

config.explanation: Molarity = moles of solute per litre of solution, mol/L.

elements.text: Now the actual job — turning this stock solution into a dilution series for Friday. How do I figure out the volumes?
The moles of solute don't change when you dilute, only the volume does — so concentration times volume before equals concentration times volume after: C1V1 = C2V2.

config.prompt: The stock solution is 2.0 mol/L. Using C1V1 = C2V2, what volume of stock (in mL) is needed to prepare 500 mL of a 0.40 mol/L solution?

config.question: Diluting a solution by adding more solvent:

options.text: Decreases the concentration, but the moles of solute stay the same
Increases the moles of solute
Makes the solute disappear entirely
Has no effect on the solution at all

config.explanation: Dilution spreads the same amount of solute over a larger volume — moles stay fixed, concentration drops.

elements.text: Dissolving explained, the crystallization mystery solved, and the dilution series calculated correctly. Everything's ready for Friday.
The series is ready, but a couple of the calculations need a second look. Let's revisit the dilution formula before next time.

elements.prompt: The dilution series is prepared. What now?

options.text: Show Priya how to read the solubility curve and use C1V1=C2V2 so this never trips her up again.
Log the results and move on. Good enough for today.

elements.text: So it was never broken — the curve just told me exactly what would happen, and the dilution formula does the rest of the work. I can predict all of this now instead of guessing.

ending.title: Saturation Solver
ending.description: Explained the crystallization from the solubility curve and prepared a correct dilution series, teaching Priya both along the way.
